data.hypothesis: A guarded SSE2 scan that checks four adjacent 16-byte vectors as one 64-byte ASCII superblock may amortize scan-loop overhead relative to earlier 16-byte scans on long ASCII spans. If any byte in a superblock has its high bit set, the unchanged scalar scanner finds and validates it, including stray continuation bytes. The official mixed-width n=65536 workload must determine whether larger blocks help or merely add overhead.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use the prior T2 outcomes as motivation for testing a different block granularity, not as evidence that SIMD is inherently slower.
memory_lessons.claim: The baseline measured 49.623 µs mean; the two prior valid T2 SIMD candidates measured 60.430 µs and 77.825 µs mean. Neither established a speedup.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this 64-byte grouped scan on the official mixed-width workload and run the official ASCII and malformed-boundary checks.

data.notes: This is a distinct T2 block-width experiment, not T1 whole-buffer validation or a hybrid. The SIMD loads are issued only when at least 64 bytes remain; a mixed block and shorter tail use the scalar path. The strict decoder, ABI, output, and thread budget are unchanged. No candidate measurement or correctness result is claimed; prior variants passed their recorded checks but were slower than baseline.
transformations: Added a compile-time-guarded SSE2 scan that loads four 16-byte vectors only when at least 64 bytes remain, combines them to test whether the full 64-byte block is ASCII, and skips the block only when every byte is ASCII.
Retained scalar ASCII scanning, strict UTF-8 decoding, scalar tail handling, ABI, output, and thread budget.
